US, Iran reportedly discussing phased deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz and end blockade
See more of our coverage in your search results.
US and Iranian negotiators are exploring a phased cease-fire deal aimed at opening the Strait of Hormuz and lifting Washington’s economic blockade on Tehran, according to multiple reports.
Delegates from the two warring countries met on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly Thursday to discuss a deal similar to the memorandum of understanding struck in mid-June, sources told Reuters.
The negotiating teams fear that because neither side wants to surrender its leverage first, the only hope for peace is to secure a phased deal.
“One way forward would be to solve the crisis in stages. The first would be to end the blockade and reopen Hormuz,” a senior Iranian official told Reuters.
A US official told The Post the talks were “positive” and “constructive,” with the US in a strong position to negotiate as it continues to escort ships through the Strait of Hormuz.
While top Iranian officials have ruled out making concessions to the US, the fact that they are now willing to negotiate suggests Tehran has recognized the pain inflicted on its economy under the American blockade and sanctions, a White House official claimed.
“Iran is desperate for a deal, President Trump holds all the cards and will make whatever decision is best for the United States,” the US official said.
Iranian officials, however, rejected the characterization and said Tehran would be ready for all outcomes, including war, if a deal isn’t reached.
“Our fingers are on the trigger,” an Iranian official told Reuters. “The Americans know what they need to do but, because of their excessive demands, the chances of diplomacy resolving this are extremely low.”
The discussions come as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters in New York that he offered a new, seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the US met certain conditions.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian reiterated that the strait would not be reopened until US sanctions and the naval blockade were cleared.
Trump, meanwhile, warned earlier this week that he could choose to “annihilate” Iran as peace negotiations stalled.
Despite the threats and recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, talks of a peace deal have helped ease surging oil prices on Friday.

The Brent futures benchmark fell to $105.46 on Friday morning, down by 1.1%, with the West Texas Intermediate seeing a similar fall to $93.56.
With Post wires

Word of an offer from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program is emerging from the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia’s top cleric issued a rare statement, calling on the kingdom’s troops to defend the country from neighboring Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
In New York, where the wars in Iran and Gaza have dominated the U.N. agenda, the leaders of Iraq, Lebanon and Egypt were scheduled to address world leaders later Friday.
Here is a look at the latest news from the Middle East. More coverage of the U.N. General Assembly is available here.
Proposal to reopen strait, resume nuclear talks on the table
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi confirmed Friday reporting that Tehran has put forth a seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program if the U.S. meets the conditions it has laid out. Talking to reporters at the U.N., Araghchi said the plan was delivered to Washington through Qatari mediators on the sidelines of the General Assembly. “If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” he said. “The choice now rests with the United States.” The seven-day clock will begin when the U.S. accepts the plan, Araghchi added. The White House said earlier Friday that U.S. officials are having positive and constructive conversations with mediators on the Iran war
Top religious figure urges Saudi troops to be ready to defend the kingdom
With Saudi oil facilities, cities and ships off its coast coming under escalating attacks, the kingdom's top religious authority has called on soldiers to be prepared to defend the country from Iran-backed Houthis.
Grand Mufti Sheikh Saleh al-Fawzan, who traditionally avoids weighing in on politics in a country that holds enormous influence among Muslims worldwide, issued the strongly worded statement. Al-Fawzan addressed his message to soldiers defending the kingdom's borders and members of the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen, peppering it with Quranic verses and religious edicts.
“Protecting this great nation, guarding its borders, defending against aggression and punishing those who want to harm any inch of it is one of the greatest duties,” he said.
The head of Yemen's internationally recognized government, Rashad al-Alimi, likewise urged Yemenis to rally behind Saudi-backed armed forces and allied groups in their fight with the Houthis.
Al-Alimi, who chairs the country’s Presidential Leadership Council, also called on Yemenis fighting alongside the Houthis to defect, announcing a general amnesty.
Al-Alimi says goal is to retake capital Sanaa from Houthis
Al-Alimi said the aim of the fighting is to restore his government’s control over Sanaa, the capital, which the Houthis seized in 2014.
His call to arms came during his first speech since his Saudi-backed forces were routed from the western Red Sea coast by the Houthis’ lightning advance on the city of Mokha and islands in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, where 12% of the world's trade passes.
The swift Houthi advances raised questions about the effectiveness of the Saudi-backed forces in the face of the disciplined, well-armed Houthis. The Houthi assault exploited divisions among the Saudi-backed forces and distrust among its leaders, leading to a chaotic troop withdrawal before the fall of Mokha.
Al-Alimi’s speech came on the 64th anniversary of the military coup that ousted the monarchy ruling northern Yemen, rooted in the Zaydi Shiite sect to which the Houthis also belong. The Houthis battled Yemen’s central government for years before sweeping down from their northern stronghold and seizing Sanaa.
Pakistani, Saudi and Turkish military chiefs hold first joint meeting
The first joint meeting of the military chiefs of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey was held in Riyadh on Friday, following the signing of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement by the three countries, Pakistan’s military said in a statement.
The chiefs of defense forces and chiefs of general staff from the three countries reviewed the regional security situation and threats facing Saudi Arabia, according to the statement.
“They strongly resented the attacks targeting the Holy City of Mecca and civilian and economic infrastructure,” the statement said.
The military chiefs also praised the vigilance and professionalism of the Saudi armed forces in ensuring the safety of the people and security of the kingdom, it said.
Iran's president says he supports Xi's call for return to MOA
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday in a post on X that Tehran supports Chinese President Xi Jinping’s call for a return to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding and renewed diplomacy between Iran and the United States.
Pezeshkian said he appreciated Xi’s “thoughtful and responsible support” for resolving differences through dialogue and diplomacy, adding that Iran backed returning to the understanding and honoring previously agreed commitments.
The post came a day after Pezeshkian met with Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. Sharif said Pezeshkian told him the Islamabad memorandum remained “fully acceptable” to Iran and that Tehran was ready to take it forward.
The 14-point memorandum, mediated by Pakistan and signed in June, provided a framework for ending the conflict.
UN Security Council demands halt to attacks by Houthi rebels
In a statement approved by its 15 members, the U.N.’s most powerful body condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and against commercial shipping in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The council called for “practical cooperation,” including with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, to prevent the Houthis from obtaining weapons, military material and training enabling them to carry out attacks.
It reminded all countries of their obligation to implement the U.N. arms embargo against the Houthis.
2 Israeli soldiers are killed in Gaza
Israel’s military said two of its soldiers were killed in northern Gaza on Thursday while inspecting an unexploded Israeli drone near a military post. They were the first Israeli soldiers killed in Gaza in months.
Five other Israeli soldiers have been killed since last October’s ceasefire that attempted to halt a more than two-year war between Israel and the militant Hamas group.
While the heaviest fighting has subsided, almost daily Israeli fire has continued. Israeli forces have carried out repeated airstrikes and frequently fire on Palestinians near military-held zones and have killed 1,408 Palestinians, according to Gaza health officials.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

US, Iran explore phased deal to end conflict as Hormuz, economic sanctions become bargaining chips
Mail This Article
US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran, according to sources close to the talks.
The talks face a big obstacle as neither side wants to be the first to surrender its leverage, according to comments to Reuters by two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomatic sources, but behind Iran's stance is a recognition of the economic cost of prolonged confrontation.
A senior Iranian official said the most plausible way to end the impasse would be a phased arrangement, with Iran allowing navigation through Hormuz in return for the US lifting its economic blockade and Tehran potentially gaining access to frozen assets.
"One way forward would be to solve the crisis in stages. The first would be to end the blockade and reopen Hormuz," he said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
That would involve US President Donald Trump accepting another temporary fix, after an earlier understanding collapsed in July. So a central challenge facing the negotiators is not just to sketch out a deal but also to ensure any concessions are durable enough for both sides to trust, the sources said.
Trump has said he thinks the US and Iran could reach a deal after midterm elections to Congress on November 3. A senior European official said the Iranians "have a very long list of demands."
A White House official said that while "Iran is desperate for a deal, President Trump holds all the cards and will make whatever decision is best for the United States." Trump, he said, remained "open to talking with Iran under the right circumstances" but had no need to negotiate, and the US was in a "very strong position" with control of the Strait of Hormuz and an Iranian economy that was "collapsing."
The official said "crushing sanctions" and "one of the most successful blockades in history" have crippled Iran’s economy and left Iran completely broke. Trump was content to let the "inevitable Iranian collapse" play out rather than be "played" by Tehran, the official said.
A deal before the midterms could benefit Trump, as reopening Hormuz could ease tensions in the Gulf, contain oil prices and help bring down politically sensitive US gasoline prices.
Iran's chances of gaining much-needed economic relief may be greater while Trump still has a greater political incentive to strike a bargain.
Leverage as obstacle?
 The leverage that brought Washington and Tehran back to negotiations could also make compromise harder.
Washington controls the pressure that is hurting Tehran most, while Tehran controls access to a critical energy chokepoint. Neither side wants to surrender that leverage without extracting something tangible in return.
This means the midterms may be less a deadline for diplomacy than for preserving the conditions that make the diplomatic efforts possible. If Washington and Tehran cannot turn leverage into a deal before the midterms, the diplomatic window could narrow as the risk of escalation grows.
Even as it seeks a diplomatic off-ramp, Tehran is preparing for the possibility of renewed war with Washington, the Iranian official said, accusing the US of using the economic blockade and threat of force as tools of coercion.
"Our fingers are on the trigger,” said the senior Iranian official. “The Americans know what they need to do but, because of their excessive demands, the chances of diplomacy resolving this are extremely low.”
Regional sources said Tehran was willing to drop a demand for payment of transit fees to use the Strait of Hormuz from the main agreement and put the demand in a side attachment instead, as ending the blockade had become the more urgent priority.
Gulf states have rejected the proposal for payment of transit fees. Any arrangement would be temporary, not a formal abandonment of Iran’s position, the regional sources said.
The US has tightened the economic vice on Iran, layering new sanctions on top of a blockade that has choked off Iran's oil exports, an important source of hard currency.

US And Iran Explore Phased Deal To Reopen Strait Of Hormuz And Lift US Blockade Of Iran
The United States and Iran are discussing a phased deal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the US economic blockade of Iran, according to sources close to the talks in New York.
Under the plan being discussed, Iran would allow ships to pass through the strait while the US would lift its economic blockade. Iran could also get access to some frozen assets.
Hormuz has become the main issue in efforts to end the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict.
Iran wants relief from the US blockade, which has put heavy pressure on its economy. The US wants ships to move freely through the waterway, a major route for global oil supplies that is now blocked by Iran.
Neither side wants to give up its leverage first, according to two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomatic sources who spoke to Reuters.
A senior Iranian official said a phased deal could be a way to break the deadlock.
The plan would mean US President Donald Trump accepting another temporary deal after an earlier understanding fell apart in July.
This month, Washington targeted Iran’s remaining commercial airlines and support networks. The move was part of a campaign to cut economic lifelines supporting the Iranian government and the powerful Revolutionary Guards.
Trump has warned that Iran’s economy could “rot” unless Tehran reaches a deal.
A White House official said Iran was desperate for a deal. But the official said Trump had no need to negotiate and would make whatever decision was best for the United States.
The official said Trump remained “open to talking with Iran under the right circumstances”.
Iran may put transit fee demand aside
Iran’s demand for transit fees for ships using Hormuz is also part of the talks.
Regional sources said Tehran was ready to remove the demand from the main agreement and put it in a separate attachment.
Ending the US blockade had become more important for Iran, the sources said.
Gulf states have rejected the proposal for transit fees.
The regional sources said putting the issue aside would only be temporary and would not mean Iran had given up its position.
The senior Iranian official said Iran was mainly concerned with keeping its administrative control over the waterway.
Gulf states have rejected Iranian control of Hormuz. They have called for freedom of navigation to be restored.
Midterm elections
Trump has said the US and Iran could reach a deal after the November 3 congressional midterm elections.
Former US negotiator Dennis Ross said he saw only a 30% chance of a deal being reached before the vote.
But Ross said both sides could have stronger reasons to reach an agreement before the elections rather than afterwards.
A deal before the midterms could reduce tensions in the Gulf, contain oil prices and help lower US gasoline prices, which are politically sensitive.
Iran could also have a better chance of getting economic relief while Trump has a stronger political reason to reach a deal.
Ross said Trump could face fewer limits after the elections and could be more willing to increase pressure on Iran or consider military options.
